q: A process of making a magnetic material into a magnet is called magnetisation.
e: True. A process of making a magnetic material into a magnet is called magnetisation. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: Two types of magnetisation are magnetisation by stroking and magnetisation using alternating current.
e: False. The two common magnetising methods are stroking and using direct current in a solenoid, not alternating current.

q: The best way to make powerful magnets is to use the magnetic effect of an electric current.
e: True. The best way to make powerful magnets is to use the magnetic effect of an electric current. Current is charge passing a point per second.

q: A steel bar is placed inside a solenoid and a direct current is passed through the solenoid.
e: True. A steel bar is placed inside a solenoid and a direct current is passed through the solenoid. A steel bar is placed inside a solenoid and a direct current is passed through the solenoid is the flow of electric charge.

q: The solenoid produces a magnetic field that magnetises the steel bar permanently.
e: True. The solenoid produces a magnetic field that magnetises the steel bar permanently. A magnetic field line leaves the north pole and returns into the south pole.

q: When the current through the solenoid is switched off, the steel bar loses its magnetism immediately.
e: False. Steel keeps magnetism when the solenoid current is switched off. Soft iron loses it quickly.

q: If an iron bar is placed instead of steel bar, the iron bar becomes magnetised temporarily (electromagnet).

q: The polarities of the magnet produced depend on the direction of electric current.
e: True. The polarities of the magnet produced depend on the direction of electric current. Current is charge passing a point per second.

q: In magnetisation by stroking, the bar is stroked several times in alternating directions along its length.
e: False. In stroking you stroke repeatedly in one direction along the bar, not back and forth.

q: The magnet (or) magnets must be lifted high above the bar between successive strokes.
e: True. The magnet (or) magnets must be lifted high above the bar between successive strokes. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: The end of the steel bar where the strokes finish always has the opposite polarity to that of the end of the stroking magnet in contact with it.
e: True. The end of the steel bar where the strokes finish always has the opposite polarity to that of the end of the stroking magnet in contact with it. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: When a piece of unmagnetised magnetic material is brought near to the pole of a permanent magnet, it is repelled by the magnet.
e: False. When a piece of unmagnetised magnetic material becomes a magnet itself after being brought near to a permanent magnet, this is called induced magnetism. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: When a piece of unmagnetised magnetic material becomes a magnet itself after being brought near to a permanent magnet, this is called induced magnetism.
e: True. When a piece of unmagnetised magnetic material becomes a magnet itself after being brought near to a permanent magnet, this is called induced magnetism. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: The north pole of the permanent magnet induces an $N$-pole in the near end of the soft iron.
e: False. A north pole induces a south pole in the near end of the soft iron. The near end is opposite, not the same.
